title: Ultimate Bishop
reviewNotes: Reconstructed the seven-piece final phase after ...Ke5: Ka4 Be7 d7 e6 against Ke5 Rd2 c5. Three checked branches show Bd6+ with either rook or king capture, and the drawing premature promotion. The preceding nine-piece sequence is context; no FEN inferred from automatic-caption square names.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to find the incredible win that the white has in this position. At first glance, it seems like white is only two steps away from getting a new queen, but it is not as simple as it might seem. Black still has an entire rook that can stop the pawns. And for example, capturing here would be a blunder. Now after the rook takes, it is always going to protect the promotion square. So white has to be careful and start by pushing the pawn to E7. [music] Now of course the pawn has to be stopped from promoting. And the only real way to do that is with rook to D2. Going behind the pawn, but allowing bishop to E5 check, which forks the king and the knight. And after the king moves, white can pick up at least one of the pieces that black had. King to D3. This doesn't make any sense, right? Can't white just promote to a new queen with a check? But after this, we are not going to have a win because there is the brilliant king to C4. A majestic idea that sacrifices the rook, but of course if the rook is taken, this would be a stalemate. The king is not in check, but is not checkmated and there are no legal moves available. So this would be a draw. But there are no other moves available to white that both save the queen from the attack of the rook and defend against checkmate on A2. So actually this should not be allowed, but sometimes the best way to reply to a brilliancy is with a counter brilliancy. And indeed, the only winning move that white has in this position is bishop to F6. If black takes, after we promote with check, there is not going to be a stalemate trap. We can just take this rook and black still has legal moves with this pawn, so we would win. But not all cards have been dealt because black can keep going and plays king to e4, because now, after bishop takes e7 and king e5, we run into a problem. We still cannot promote to a new queen. Black is just going to take the queen, take the pawn, and this is going to be yet again a draw. So, is this it? Is black simply out of the woods in this position? Well, not exactly. White has a one last, incredible, and ingenious idea [music] in this position. Bishop to d6. This is a check, but it's also stepping in the way of the rook, meaning that if the king takes, white can just promote and very easily win. But, if the rook takes, with only two pawns left, white plays e7. And unfortunately for the rook, it is simply impossible to prevent both promotions at the same time. The best that black can do is collect one of the pawns, allow white to promote, and hope that white will not know how to convert this winning end game.
